paper_title: ForcingBooster: Adaptive Patch-wise Denoising for Fast Autoregressive Video Diffusion

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Autoregressive video diffusion models have become a leading approach to real-time interactive video generation and video world modeling. However, existing methods typically allocate computation uniformly across space when generating the next video chunk, updating all patches with the same denoising schedule and number of function evaluations. This ignores the spatial heterogeneity of video content: static, simple, or recurring regions are often easier to denoise, while other regions require further refinement or additional context. A uniform budget thus leads to redundant computation on easy patches, whereas reducing the fixed step count can leave difficult patches insufficiently refined. We introduce \methodname{}, a general framework that dynamically allocates denoising steps to individual patches: easy patches stop early to improve efficiency, while difficult patches receive more refinement steps. This design accelerates generation with negligible quality degradation. Our method is compatible with most existing few-step autoregressive diffusion models, requiring only a lightweight routing module with modest training. Experiments demonstrate that \methodname{} reduces the total number of denoising steps applied across video patches by about 50\% while maintaining visual quality comparable to the four-step baseline.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Video generation Wan et al. (2025); HaCohen et al. (2026) is becoming core approach for digital content creation Liang et al. (2025), scene simulation Sun et al. (2024); Wen et al. (2023), and interactive video world modeling Team et al. (2026); Yuan et al. (2026b). Despite their different goals, these applications all require models to preserve visual quality while responding to input signals and generating future content with low latency. Recent video diffusion models have substantially improved generation quality, yet their iterative sampling process remains too slow for real-time interaction. Bridging this qualitylatency gap is therefore central challenge for real-time video generation and video world models. Autoregressive video diffusion converts joint full-video generation into sequence of next-chunk predictions by introducing causal attention. These methods (Chen et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2026) partition video into short temporal chunks and generate each chunk conditioned on the preceding ones. Once the first chunk is generated, the model can begin producing output and continue with subsequent chunks. This allows the model to output completed chunks without waiting for the entire video. Causal attention enables the use of KV caching to avoid repeatedly processing previous chunks. Distillation methods Yin et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2025); Zhu et al. (2026); Zhao et al. (2026b) further reduce the generation time of each chunk, compressing models that require dozens of denoising steps into autoregressive generators that use four steps or fewer. Recent methods reduce computation by compressing historical context Yuan et al. (2026a) or choosing the number of denoising steps for entire frames or chunks Le et al. (2026). Although these methods substantially reduce the denoising iterations required for each frame or chunk, they typically assign the same denoising schedule and computational budget to all latent patches within that chunk. Every new chunk still requires complete multi-step diffusion process. Some work has explored different denoising schedules across spatial regions in reasoning and image generation Wewer et al. (2025); Schusterbauer et al. (2026). Our analysis indicates that some patches produce predictions close to the full denoising result at earlier steps, while others still require further refinement. For example, as shown in Fig. 1(a), fewer denoising steps are allocated to the background water (blue), while more are allocated to the moving climber and the textured rock face (red). In Fig. 1(b), as the camera pans left, the sky and the large building on the right receive fewer steps, whereas the trees and newly revealed structures on the left receive more. Applying all steps to every patch therefore wastes computation on patches that are already stable, whereas reducing the step count for the entire chunk can degrade regions that still need refinement. Consequently, even when the base model has already been distilled to very few steps, allocating computation according to local content still offers substantial room for improvement. We propose ForcingBooster, which equips an existing few-step autoregressive generator with lightweight router that dynamically determines which latent patches require further denoising at each step. The router examines each patch in the context of the generated history and the current conditioning signals, such as camera poses or text controls, to assess whether its prediction has already sufficiently converged. Patches deemed complete stop denoising, while only the remaining uncertain or condition-sensitive regions continue to be refined. In this way, ForcingBooster allocates computation adaptively across space and denoising steps, reducing redundant refinement without modifying the generator itself. Two key challenges arise in enabling patch-wise early stopping. First, if patch terminates before completing the full denoising schedule, we need valid clean latent that can be directly used as its output. To address this, we observe that diffusion and flow-matching generators admit clean-latent estimate at every intermediate denoising step, either predicted directly or recovered from their native parameterization. This intermediate ˆx0 prediction provides natural output for early-exited patches, allowing different regions to terminate at different denoising steps without modifying the original sampling schedule. Second, there is no ground-truth supervision indicating when each patch should stop. We therefore formulate router learning as trade-off between generation quality and computation. Specifically, we introduce stopping surrogate loss that penalizes high stop probabilities when the current cleanlatent prediction deviates from the full-step denoised latent, together with computational loss that encourages patches to terminate with fewer denoising steps. These objectives are optimized with onpolicy rollouts of the current router, so the estimated continuation cost reflects its evolving routing 2 behavior. The full-step outputs of the frozen generator serve as training references, enabling the router to be trained without additional video data or manually defined stopping labels. We validate ForcingBooster across video generation and world models with different scales and architectures, ranging from camera-conditioned world models to real-time interactive autoregressive video generators. On average, the router requires only approximately 500 training steps and reduces the total number of denoising steps applied across video patches by about 50%, while maintaining VBench scores comparable to those of the corresponding four-step baselines.

sections.title: 2.1 AUTOREGRESSIVE VIDEO DIFFUSION
sections.content: Autoregressive video diffusion generates temporal chunks conditioned on earlier ones. Diffusion Forcing trains causal models with independent noise levels across tokens Chen et al. (2024). Later work improves long video generation through history management and noise scheduling Yang et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025b), or trains on generated histories to reduce error accumulation Po et al. (2025); Guo et al. (2026); Cui et al. (2025). Other work studies multiplayer world modeling Savva et al. (2026) and flexible chunking and generation orders Ma et al. (2026a). 2.2 DIFFUSION DISTILLATION AND POST-TRAINING Few-step distillation reduces the number of denoiser evaluations. DMD and DMD2 distill diffusion models through distribution matching Yin et al. (2024b;a); Zhao et al. (2026a), and CausVid extends this approach to autoregressive video generation Yin et al. (2025). Self Forcing trains on generated histories Huang et al. (2025), while Causal Forcing uses an autoregressive teacher for initialization Zhu et al. (2026). Further work studies generation in one or two steps Zhao et al. (2026b); Feng et al. (2026), flexible sampling budgets Gu et al. (2026), diversity preservation Chen et al. (2026), and reward supervision Lu et al. (2025). Recent on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) methods use richer teacher context to supervise the models own rollouts Jiang et al. (2026); Liu et al. (2026a), while DanceOPD Zhou et al. (2026) learns from expert velocity fields on student-generated states. These methods update the generator and typically use shared step budget across spatial patches within each frame or chunk. 2.3 ADAPTIVE COMPUTATION FOR DIFFUSION Adaptive sampling selects denoising budgets for individual samples Zhang et al. (2024), while spatial reasoning models allow different regions to follow different denoising schedules Wewer et al. (2025). Other methods reduce computation within each denoiser evaluation Zhao et al. (2024); You et al. (2025) or process fewer tokens through history compression and multiscale generation Yuan et al. (2026a). Caching methods reuse intermediate features across denoising steps Ma et al. (2023); Lv et al. (2025). TeaCache estimates output changes from inputs modulated by timestep embeddings to guide reuse Liu et al. (2025a), while AdaCache adapts cache intervals using video features Kahatapitiya et al. (2024). Other methods selectively recompute tokens or regions Zou et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2026b); Xu et al. (2026), extend caching to autoregressive video chunks Ma et al. (2026b), or adjust cache thresholds during denoising Agrawal et al. (2026). DSA Le et al. (2026) jointly trains confidence head and the generator to select denoising steps for entire frames or chunks, but spatial patches within each unit still share the same budget. Patch Forcing Schusterbauer et al. (2026) trains image generators with spatially varying noise levels and uses predicted patch difficulty to guide sampling. HSA Chu & Patel (2026) assigns token-level step budgets without training and preserves KV context, while continuing to update skipped latents with cached velocities. In contrast, ForcingBooster learns patch-wise stopping in frozen few-step autoregressive generator, allowing easy regions to finish early while retaining further refinement for difficult ones. We train only lightweight router and retain the original denoising schedule. Training balances reconstruction error against denoising cost using full-step references and histories generated under the current routing policy. Rather than advancing skipped latents with cached velocities, 3 Figure 2: Adaptive patch-wise inference and on-policy router training. (a) The router selects patches to continue denoising; stopped predictions provide reusable KV context. (b) no-gradient rollout records exits for replay. Reconstruction and computational costs train the router through its stopping probabilities. we fix each stopped patchs clean latent prediction. Sparse inference then removes it from subsequent Transformer updates once its KV cache is built. This reduces redundant computation without discarding the context needed by active patches and subsequent chunks.

sections.title: 3 METHOD
sections.content: 3.1 PRELIMINARY AND OVERVIEW ForcingBooster is designed to improve the efficiency of an existing autoregressive video generator with router that allocates an adaptive denoising budget for different regions. Specifically, we will first introduce the x0-prediction mechanism of diffusion or flow matching models, which will be used in our denoising router to early terminate the denoising process for well generated patches. x0-prediction of autoregressive video generator. The generator produces videos chunk by chunk in latent space in an autoregressive manner. Each chunk starts from Gaussian noise x1 and follows fixed schedule {tk}K k=1 with t0 = 1, tK = 0. We express the denoising process at step as ˆx0,tk+1 = Gθ (xtk , tk; H, y) , xtk+1 = Etk+1 (ˆx0,tk+1 ) = 1, . . . , K, (1) where Gθ is the denoising network with parameters θ, xtk is the noisy input at noise level tk, denotes generation conditions, denotes the generation history represented by the KV cache of previously generated frames, ˆx0,tk+1 is the predicted clean latent at this step, and Etk+1 maps this clean prediction to the next noisy state xtk+1 . This formulation abstracts over the specific parameterization used by diffusion or flow-matching models: even when the network predicts noise or velocity, an equivalent clean-latent estimate ˆx0,tk+1 can be obtained at each step. Importantly, this intermediate clean prediction allows patch to terminate denoising early and directly use its current ˆx0,tk as the final latent prediction. 4 Figure 3: Denoising steps required by different patches. Left: fixed-step generation results with enlarged local details. Right: patch-wise first-hit step distribution at 35 dB PSNR relative to the four-step reference in separate controlled experiment. Denoising router. vanilla autoregressive video generator will use the same number of denoising steps for every patch in the current generation chunk. However, different patches may require substantially different amounts of denoising budget. In particular, regions that can be reliably inferred from the generation history may converge much earlier than newly revealed or conditiondependent regions. To exploit this redundancy, ForcingBooster applies denoising router that predicts stop probability pi,k for all patches after every denoising step. Then, for patches with large stop probability, we will stop denoising these patches in the subsequent steps, use their predicted clean latents ˆx0,tk at this step as the output, and further store the KV caches of these patches to for the denoising of other non-stopped patches. In the following, we describe how our router changes and speeds up the generation process (Section 3.3) and how we train our router with surrogate loss (Section 3.4). 3.2 DENOISING STEPS REQUIRED BY DIFFERENT PATCHES few-step schedule reduces the number of denoising updates, but still applies the same step count to every patch. Some patches may already be close to the full-step output while others still need further updates. If this difference exists, we may be able to reduce computation selectively rather than shorten the schedule for all patches. We therefore conduct controlled experiment to examine when each patchs prediction first approaches the full-step output. We use Causal Forcing Zhu et al. (2026) as the base model, fix the context to the first ground-truth video chunk, and generate only the immediately following target chunk. Each target chunk contains three latent frames. We hold the generation conditions, initial noise, and noise between denoising steps fixed and record the clean latent prediction at each step of single four-step sampling run. We decode each prediction and compute the peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) against the decoded four-step output over the region corresponding to each patch. We record the first step at which this score reaches 35 dB. This measures agreement with the generators own full-step output, rather than reconstruction of the ground-truth video. As shown in Fig. 3 (right), 30.60% of patches reach the threshold after the first step. further 12.25% and 9.69% first reach it at the second and third steps, respectively. The remaining 47.45% do not reach it within the first three steps. Figure 3 (left) shows the final frames from separate fixed-step generation runs with the same seed. Each run uses four steps for the first chunk and the indicated step count for subsequent chunks. The sky and hillside look broadly similar across the results, whereas the enlarged hand and forearm show clear differences. With one step, the hand is poorly defined. Two and three steps recover more of its shape, but visible distortions remain around the hand and wrist compared with the four-step result. These results show that patches within the same chunk approach the full-step output at different rates. They motivate reducing later updates at positions already close to that output while allowing other positions to continue denoising.

sections.title: 3.3 ADAPTIVE PATCH-WISE DENOISING ROUTER
sections.content: After each denoising step, the router predicts stop probability for each patch to stop the denoising of well-generated patches. Then, we add the KV cache of these stopped patches to the history and proceed to the next denoising step. Stop probability prediction. Let Ak denote the active patches at the beginning of step and A0 includes all patches. After the denoising step k, the router Rϕ reuses hidden features uk from the generators last transformer layer to predict the stop probability pi,k by where ϕ denotes the router parameters. threshold η is used to determine the active patches Ak+1 pi,k = [Rϕ(uk)]i , Ak. (2) Ak+1 = {i Ak pi,k η} , < K. (3) As shown in Fig. 2(a), only Ak+1 will be used in the denoising of the next step. For patches stopped at this step, their ˆx0,tk+1 from Eq. (1) are used as output. Meanwhile, the KV values of these stopped patches will be stored into the KV cache to help the denoising of the remaining patches. Computation reduction. The router progressively reduces the number of active patches throughout denoising. Once patch stops, it is removed from subsequent denoising updates and its key-value representations are cached for reuse. Therefore, later denoising steps only compute new representations for the remaining active patches, while stopped patches continue to provide contextual information through the KV cache without being recomputed. As more patches terminate, the active set shrinks monotonically, reducing the per-step computation and accelerating the generation. 3.4 ON-POLICY ROUTER TRAINING Learning the stop probability. Training the router is non-trivial because there is no ground-truth annotation indicating at which denoising step each patch should stop. Instead of constructing discrete stopping labels, we directly relate the stop probability to the quality of the current clean-latent Intuitively, if the predicted clean latent ˆx0,tk at step is already close to the target prediction. clean latent, further denoising brings little benefit and the router should assign high stop probability. Conversely, large prediction error indicates that the patch still requires further refinement and should receive low stop probability. Based on this observation, we introduce differentiable surrogate loss and denoising cost loss to train the router. Stopping surrogate loss. Let 0 denote the target clean latent, and let measure the prediction error of patch after step k. We penalize stopping in proportion to this error: di,k = (cid:13) (cid:13)ˆx (cid:13) 0,tk x,i 0 (cid:13) 2 (cid:13) (cid:13) 2 (4) Lstop = 1 Ak (cid:88) iAk pi,k di,k. (5) This objective discourages high stop probability when the current prediction is still inaccurate, while imposing little penalty on stopping patches with converged clean-latent predictions. Expected denoising cost. Optimizing the surrogate loss alone will lead to trivial solution in which the router assigns zero stop probability to every patch, allowing all patches to run through the complete denoising schedule. To encourage early stopping, we introduce denoising cost loss that minimizes the expected number of denoising steps for each patch. For candidate patch at step k, stopping immediately incurs cost of k, whereas continuing denoising incurs cost determined by the final stopping step ei,k of our routing policy. The denoising cost is then Lcomp = 1 Ak (cid:88) iAk [pi,k + (1 pi,k) ei,k] . (6) 6 Figure 4: Qualitative comparison. The rows show the results from four-step baseline to one-step sampling, and ForcingBooster. One-step and Two-step sampling exhibits decline in quality and visible artifacts. Red boxes indicate visual artifacts. Here, pi,k corresponds to the cost of stopping at the current step, while (1 pi,k) ei,k represents the cost of continuing until the patch eventually exits. Since ei,k > k, minimizing this objective favors larger stop probability whenever further denoising is unnecessary, thereby reducing the overall denoising computation. To estimate ei,k, we roll out the remaining denoising steps using the current router and stopping threshold η, and record when each active patch eventually exits. This onpolicy estimation allows the computational cost to reflect the behavior of the current routing policy as it evolves during training. Self-generated training targets. The target 0 can be obtained directly from the frozen generator itself, without requiring additional video data or stopping annotations. Specifically, we first run the original generator with its full denoising schedule and use the resulting clean latent as the training target, and record this trajectory. We then use this trajectory perturb this latent to randomly sampled noise level tk and feed the noisy latent, which is recorded in the trajectory, back to the frozen generator to obtain the intermediate clean prediction ˆx0,tk and the corresponding hidden features for router prediction. We refer to this process as replay. The discrepancy between ˆx0,tk and the full-step result therefore directly measures how much quality would be lost by stopping at step k. In this way, the pretrained generator provides both the training inputs and supervision for the router, allowing it to be trained without collecting any additional data.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTS
sections.content: We evaluate ForcingBooster on several video generation methods and world models, comparing generation quality and inference time with uniform fixed-step sampling. We then analyze spatial computation allocation and router settings. 4.1 IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS Our main experiments use Causal Forcing 1.3B (Zhu et al., 2026) to generate 81-frame videos at 480 832 and 16 FPS. Following its training data setup, we train only the router for 500 steps using AdamW, learning rate of 104, and global batch size of 8. The pretrained components and denoising schedule remain fixed. Following common practice Gu et al. (2026); Huang et al. (2025); Zhu et al. (2026), we adopt VBench Huang et al. (2023) to evaluate generated videos across 16 fine-grained dimensions. We report the aggregated Quality and Semantic scores, together with their weighted combination, the Total score. For this model, inference uses single A800 GPU with BF16 precision and batch size 1. We report mean end-to-end generation time, including text encoding, the first chunk, router execution, KV cache construction, and VAE decoding. 7 Table 1: Comparison on Causal Forcing checkpoint. The original four-step sampler (vanilla) without routing serves as the baseline. All methods use four steps for the first chunk and apply their respective strategies to subsequent chunks. Fixed-step baselines execute prefix of the original schedule and return the clean latent prediction from the last executed step. Generation conditions and noise are matched across methods. Table 1 shows that ForcingBooster achieves 1.3 end-to-end speedup reduces the total number of denoising steps applied across video patches by about 50%, while retaining Quality and Total scores close to the four-step baseline and an almost unchanged Semantic score. At runtime similar to uniform two-step sampling, it also achieves higher scores on all three metrics, showing the benefit of allocating denoising steps across patches rather than reducing them uniformly. The qualitative comparison in Fig. 4 reveals clearer advantage of ForcingBooster than the quantitative results suggest. The one-step, two-step, and three-step baselines all produce artifacts in regions with complex textures. In contrast, ForcingBooster computes more on these patches and avoids artifacts. 4.3 FURTHER EVALUATION We further evaluate Wan2.1 14B, LingBot-World-V2, and LongLive. The qualitative comparison in Fig. also indicates that one-step sampling results exhibit artifacts and decline in quality across various models. sections.title: 4.4 PATCH-WISE ALLOCATION
sections.content: We compare different computation allocation strategies to examine whether the improvement in generation quality comes from effectively selecting spatial positions. Random preserves the distribution of exit steps within each latent frame but randomly permutes the spatial positions assigned to those steps. Chunk-wise router aggregates patch-wise exit decisions into uniform number of denoising steps for each chunk. We compare these two strategies with ForcingBooster and the original four-step baseline. At comparable runtimes, ForcingBooster achieves higher Total score than both alternatives  (Table 3)  . The comparison with Random shows that the locations of early exits matter, not just their step-count distribution. The improvement over Chunk-wise router further supports assigning different step counts within the same chunk to preserve generation quality. Fig. 6 shows the four methods at multiple time points under the same generation conditions. Chunk-wise router produces blurry frames in chunks assigned fewer denoising steps, with weaker details in regions such as the face and hands. Random exhibits severe flickering and detail loss in the generated video, with unstable local structures in the person and objects over time. In contrast, ForcingBooster better preserves visual sharpness and temporal consistency, producing results closest overall to four-step baseline. 9 Figure 7: Router analysis. (b) Effect of the stopping threshold η, with separate router trained for each threshold and the same threshold used at inference. Both panels report LPIPS against the four-step output and normalized full-video runtime; lower is better. (a) Effect of the computational cost weight λnfe.

sections.title: 4.5 ROUTER ANALYSIS
sections.content: We study the computational cost weight λnfe and stopping threshold η. We measure agreement with the four-step output using LPIPS and report full-video runtime normalized by the four-step baseline. Computational cost. We vary λnfe in the training objective from Section 3.4. With zero or insufficient weight on Lnfe, the router retains all four steps and adds overhead without reducing runtime (Fig. 7(a)). Weights between 0.015 and 0.030 enable substantial time savings with low LPIPS. Further increases bring smaller runtime gains and larger deviations from the four-step output. These results show that sufficient cost penalty is needed to learn effective early stopping, while overemphasizing it offers limited further acceleration. Stopping threshold. We vary η from Section 3.3, training separate router for each value from 0.1 to 0.9 with λnfe = 0.030. Each router uses the same threshold during training and inference. Across these routers, higher thresholds generally increase runtime but do not consistently lower LPIPS (Fig. 7(b)). Thus, more conservative stopping threshold does not necessarily produce outputs closer to the four-step reference. Video dynamics and speedup. We quantify video dynamics using RAFT Teed & Deng (2020) to estimate optical flow between adjacent frames, averaging its magnitude over space and time. We divide the videos into five equally sized groups by this measure and report the inference speedup and patch-wise NFE reduction for each group. As shown in Fig. 7(c), ForcingBooster achieves larger speedups on lower-motion videos, approaching the runtime of one-step denoising with up to approximately 1.5 speedup or reduces the total number of denoising steps applied across video patches by about 75% over the four-step baseline.

sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We introduce ForcingBooster, general framework that dynamically allocates denoising steps to individual patches: simple patches terminate early to improve efficiency, whereas complex patches receive additional refinement steps. This design accelerates generation with negligible quality degradation. ForcingBooster is compatible with most existing few-step autoregressive diffusion models and requires only lightweight routing module and modest training, without fine-tuning the heavyweight generator or relying on additional video data.
